Transferring a spouse’s unused age, pension, disability and tuition amounts in 2026: how Schedule 2 works

A worked guide to line 32600 for 2026: which of a spouse’s or common-law partner’s credits can move to the other, how Schedule 2 decides the unused part, how it sits beside the spouse amount on line 30300, why CPP and OAS do not create a pension amount, the CAD 5,000 tuition cap, when the claimant has too little tax to use it, and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 11 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original illustration of the 2026 federal transfer of unused amounts from a spouse or common-law partner (Schedule 2, line 32600), using the 2025 schedule’s line structure with CRA’s 2026 indexed amounts. Transferable amounts are the spouse’s age amount (CAD 9,208, less 15% of net income above CAD 46,432), pension income amount (up to CAD 2,000 of eligible pension income), disability amount (CAD 10,341) and up to CAD 5,000 of current-year tuition less what they use. The spouse first uses them to bring their own federal tax to zero after the basic personal amount and the CPP, EI and Canada employment credits on employment income entered. The claimant’s credit is limited to federal tax left after their own basic, age, pension, CPP and EI credits. Net income is taken as taxable income for both people; provincial and territorial Schedule 2 amounts, the caregiver amount for infirm children (line 30500), the infirm-spouse addition to line 30300, medical expenses, donations, dividend credits and pension income splitting are left out.

The central idea

For 2026 a spouse can pass the other the part of their age amount (up to CAD 9,208), pension income amount (up to CAD 2,000), disability amount (CAD 10,341) and current-year tuition (up to CAD 5,000) that they do not need to bring their own federal tax to zero. Schedule 2 takes those amounts, subtracts the spouse’s taxable income less their basic personal amount and payroll credits, and the rest goes on line 32600. It is worth 14% federally, and only against tax the claimant actually owes.

01

What Schedule 2 moves

Most federal credits are non-refundable: they reduce tax owed, and anything a person cannot use is gone. When one spouse or common-law partner has little taxable income, several of their credits would be wasted. Line 32600 lets the other spouse claim the unused part of five of them, calculated on Schedule 2:

  • the age amount (line 30100), for a spouse 65 or older at the end of the year;
  • the Canada caregiver amount for infirm children under 18 (line 30500), if the spouse claimed it;
  • the pension income amount (line 31400);
  • the disability amount for the spouse themselves (line 31600);
  • the spouse’s current-year tuition amount, up to CAD 5,000, as designated on their T2202, TL11A or TL11C.

The 2026 figures are CRA’s published amounts after 2.0% indexation; the CAD 2,000 and CAD 5,000 caps are fixed dollar amounts. The age amount reaches zero at CAD 46,432 + 9,208 ÷ 15% ≈ CAD 107,819 of net income (derived). At 14%, a full age amount is worth CAD 1,289.12 of federal tax, the pension amount CAD 280 and the disability amount CAD 1,447.74.

02

Who can use it, and what does not count

Under the CRA rules for line 32600 you can claim the transfer if you had a spouse or common-law partner at the end of the year, they qualified for at least one of the amounts above, and they did not need all of them to reduce their federal tax to zero. You cannot claim it if you were separated because of a breakdown in the relationship for 90 days or more including 31 December. If the spouse does not file, you use the amounts they would have entered and attach their slips.

Three details often trip up households:

  • CPP, QPP and OAS are not pension income for the pension amount. Eligible pension income at 65 or older includes registered pension plan lifetime payments, RRIF and LIF payments, annuity payments and pension income split to you under an election. Under 65, it is mainly a lifetime pension from a registered pension plan, plus certain amounts received because of a spouse’s death. A 66-year-old with CPP and OAS only has no pension amount to transfer; CAD 2,000 a year from a RRIF creates the full one.
  • Only current-year tuition moves. Tuition carried forward from an earlier year stays with the student. The CAD 5,000 cap is reduced by the current-year tuition the student uses themselves, even if some of the year’s amount is still unused.
  • The age amount depends on the spouse’s own net income, not the couple’s. A spouse with CAD 60,000 of income has an age amount of CAD 9,208 − 15% × (60,000 − 46,432) = CAD 7,172.80, but with that income they would need it all.

03

How Schedule 2 works out the unused part

The schedule is short. It adds up what the spouse qualifies for, measures how much of that they need, and transfers the difference:

  1. Lines 1 to 6: add the spouse’s age amount, caregiver amount for infirm children, pension income amount, disability amount and the tuition designated to you.
  2. Line 7: the spouse’s taxable income. If it is above the top of the lowest bracket (CAD 57,375 on the 2025 form), use their federal tax on that income divided by the lowest rate instead, which turns higher-rate tax into an equivalent amount at 14.5% (14% for 2026).
  3. Lines 8 to 11: add the spouse’s basic personal amount (line 30000), their line 96 (CPP and EI credits, the Canada employment amount and a few others such as the home buyers’ amount) and the tuition they used themselves (line 32300).
  4. Line 12: line 7 minus line 11, not below zero. This is the spouse’s adjusted taxable income, the part of the five amounts they need.
  5. Line 13: line 6 minus line 12, not below zero, goes on line 32600 of your return.

The model’s default is a retired couple. The lower-income spouse is 67 with CAD 20,000 of income: CAD 16,000 of CPP and OAS and a CAD 4,000 RRIF payment. The claimant is 68 with CAD 85,000, CAD 40,000 of it from a workplace pension.

The spouse’s own federal tax is 14% × CAD 20,000 = CAD 2,800. Their basic personal amount and the CAD 3,548 of age and pension amounts they keep give 14% × CAD 20,000 = CAD 2,800 of credits, so they owe nothing federally and the CAD 7,660 they could not use moves across. The claimant has about CAD 10,559 of federal tax left after their own basic, age and pension credits, so they use the CAD 1,072.40 in full. Without the transfer that value would simply be lost.

04

The spouse amount and the transfer are separate claims

Line 30300, the spouse or common-law partner amount, is a different credit. It is the claimant’s basic personal amount (CAD 16,452 for 2026 below CAD 181,440 of the claimant’s net income) minus the spouse’s net income, and it applies at any age. The claimant can make both claims in the same year.

The first chart moves the spouse’s income with everything else fixed:

  • With no income, the spouse needs none of their amounts. The claimant gets the full CAD 16,452 spouse amount and the full age amount of CAD 9,208 on line 32600 (CAD 3,592.40 together at 14%; the pension amount is zero because there is no pension income).
  • Up to CAD 16,452, the spouse amount falls dollar for dollar, while the transfer stays complete because the spouse’s basic personal amount alone covers their income.
  • Above CAD 16,452, the spouse amount is zero and each extra dollar of the spouse’s income keeps one more dollar of age and pension amounts on their own return. In the default, the transfer reaches zero at CAD 16,452 + 9,208 + 2,000 = CAD 27,660.

So the transfer reaches further up the income scale than the spouse amount. For a pensioner couple, the spouse amount often ends with OAS and CPP alone, while line 32600 can still carry several thousand dollars of age amount.

05

What the spouse qualifies for changes the reach

The grid compares five kinds of spouse at incomes from zero to CAD 60,000, with all income treated as pension or other non-employment income:

  • Age amount only (CPP and OAS, no RRIF or pension): the full CAD 9,208 moves until the spouse’s income passes CAD 16,452, and nothing is left at CAD 25,660.
  • Age and pension amounts: CAD 11,208 at most, ending at CAD 27,660. Drawing CAD 2,000 a year from a RRIF from 65 is often enough to create the pension amount, which then transfers in part or in full.
  • Age, pension and disability: CAD 21,549 at most, and CAD 8,001 is still left at CAD 30,000 of income; the transfer ends at CAD 38,001. With 2026 rates that combination is worth up to CAD 3,016.86 to the claimant.
  • Disability amount, under 65: CAD 10,341 until the spouse’s income passes the basic personal amount, ending at CAD 26,793.
  • CAD 8,000 of tuition, under 65: at most CAD 5,000 moves. A student spouse with CAD 20,000 of income uses CAD 3,548 of the tuition themselves, transfers CAD 1,452 and carries the other CAD 3,000 forward to their own future years.

A spouse with employment income also has CPP, EI and Canada employment credits on line 96, which raise line 11 and leave more to transfer. In the model’s tuition example, a student spouse earning CAD 12,000 has CAD 18,569.35 of basic and payroll credits, more than their income, so they transfer the full CAD 5,000.

06

When the claimant cannot use it

The transfer helps only if the claimant has federal tax left after their own credits. For a retired claimant those include their own basic personal amount, their own age amount (reduced by their income) and their own pension amount. In the default, the claimant at CAD 85,000 has an age amount of CAD 3,422.80 and about CAD 10,559 of tax left.

If both spouses have CAD 20,000 of income, the claimant’s own CAD 16,452 basic, CAD 9,208 age and CAD 2,000 pension amounts already exceed their income, so the CAD 1,072.40 credit from the transfer is entirely wasted. It cannot go back to the spouse, and unused age, pension and disability amounts cannot be carried forward. The claimant-income chart shows the credit becoming usable only once the claimant’s income passes about CAD 27,660, and fully usable a little above CAD 35,000.

Schedule 2 only moves amounts the spouse cannot use. If the spouse needs all of them, line 13 is zero whatever the claimant’s income, so the transfer never pushes tax onto the lower-income spouse.

07

How it interacts with pension income splitting

Pension income splitting on Form T1032 moves up to half of eligible pension income from one spouse to the other for tax purposes. It changes both sides of Schedule 2:

  • the receiving spouse’s taxable income on line 7 rises, so they need more of their own amounts and less is left to transfer;
  • split pension income counts as eligible pension income for the receiving spouse, so a spouse with only CPP and OAS gains a pension amount of up to CAD 2,000;
  • the transferring spouse’s lower net income can increase their own age amount and reduce OAS recovery tax.

The two tools therefore do not add up simply. Tax software usually tests split percentages and then runs Schedule 2 on the result. This model holds incomes as entered and does not optimise a split; the separate pension income splitting guide models the election, including the age amount and OAS recovery.

08

Who claims it: CRA statistics

CRA’s final statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) count 1,497,600 returns with line 32600, claiming CAD 10.67 billion of amounts, about CAD 7,122 per return. For scale, 7,268,130 returns claimed an age amount, 6,024,730 a pension income amount and 2,382,380 a spouse amount.

09

Checklist and limits of the model

  • Complete the spouse’s return, or a notional one, first: Schedule 2 uses their line 30000, line 96, line 32300 and taxable income.
  • Confirm the pension amount comes from eligible pension income; CPP, QPP, OAS and GIS do not count, and a RRIF payment counts from 65.
  • Check the age amount against the spouse’s own net income, and note the year they turn 65 (born 1961 or earlier for 2026).
  • For tuition, the student designates the amount on the back of the T2202; carried-forward tuition stays with them.
  • For a new disability claim, the spouse needs an approved Form T2201.
  • Complete the provincial or territorial Schedule 2 too; provinces use their own amounts, and Quebec is separate.

The model covers federal amounts only and treats net income as taxable income. It includes the basic personal amount and the CPP, EI and Canada employment credits from employment income on the spouse’s line 11, but not the home buyers’, home accessibility, adoption or volunteer amounts, nor the caregiver amount for infirm children. The claimant’s room allows for their own basic, age, pension, CPP and EI credits but not medical expenses, donations, dividend tax credits or other claims that would also use their tax. It does not model the infirm-spouse addition to line 30300, pension splitting, OAS recovery tax or provincial credits. Use CRA’s schedules or tax software for an actual return.

  1. CRA · Line 32600 – Amounts transferred from your spouse or common-law partner ↗

    Date modified 31 August 2026 (written for 2025). Eligible amounts (lines 30100, 30500, 31400, 31600, 32300), year-end spouse condition, 90-day separation exclusion, no carried-forward tuition.

  2. CRA · Schedule 2, Federal Amounts Transferred from your Spouse or Common-Law Partner, 2025 ↗

    Lines 1 to 13: amounts transferred = total eligible amounts less (taxable income, or line 76 ÷ 14.5% above CAD 57,375, minus lines 30000, 96 and 32300); tuition maximum CAD 5,000 less current-year amounts used.

  3. CRA · Schedule 11, Federal Tuition Amount and Canada Training Credit, 2025 ↗

    Current-year tuition is used after line 101 credits; the transferable part is the lesser of CAD 5,000 and the year’s amount, less the part used.

  4. CRA · T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return 5000-R, 2025 ↗

    Step 5 Part B: line 96 adds lines 30800 to 31300 (CPP, EI, Canada employment amount and others); basic personal amount CAD 16,129 and age amount CAD 9,028 for 2025.

  5. CRA · Line 31400 – Pension income amount ↗

    Date modified 20 January 2026. Maximum CAD 2,000; eligible pension income under 65 and at 65 or older; OAS, CPP and QPP benefits do not qualify.

  6. CRA · Line 30300 – Spouse or common-law partner amount ↗

    Date modified 20 January 2026. Claimant’s basic personal amount less the spouse’s net income; claimable together with line 32600.

  7. CRA · Adjustment of personal income tax and benefit amounts ↗

    Page details 12 March 2026. 2026 indexation 2.0%: basic personal amount CAD 16,452–14,829, age amount CAD 9,208 from CAD 46,432, disability amount CAD 10,341, Canada employment amount CAD 1,501, second bracket from CAD 58,523.
